turns.voice_text:
We never were house-churches. From the very first day of our schism, we were a whole parallel church, bishop for bishop, see for see, across all of Roman North Africa. When Majorinus was consecrated against Caecilian in 311/312, it was not a small gathering breaking away to meet in someone's home -- it was one bishop set up against another bishop, over the same people, in the same city, claiming the same office. And that pattern held everywhere we went. In many towns of Roman North Africa, two churches stood where most towns elsewhere had one: one congregation gathered under a bishop of our own communion, another under a bishop of the rival, sometimes within sight of one another in the same town, the same street.

A bishop among us was chosen the same way a bishop was chosen anywhere else in the Latin church of our time -- by the clergy and people of his own see, often with neighboring bishops present to confirm the choice. Our councils gathered our own bishops and claimed the same binding authority our rival's councils claimed for themselves. At the great Conference in Carthage in 411, 279 of our own bishops sat opposite 286 of theirs. That is not a network of small gatherings. That is one whole church answering another, institution for institution.
